Female Creek chubsuckers reach a total length at puberty of 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters], a milestone typically achieved as they complete their fifth year of life. A gravid adult, having attained full somatic growth, can attain an ultimate total length of 41.9 centimeters [Li = 41.9 centimeters]. Growth trajectories derived from field surveys indicate that the length–mass relationship follows a conventional power function, with an individual at puberty weighing approximately 74.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 74.2 grams]. Fecundity assessments on reproductively active fish show that females produce roughly 79 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 79 eggs per spawning event]. Under the stable thermal regime of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] that characterizes their preferred habitats, females typically spawn once per day [F_R_i = spawn once per day], reflecting a remarkably high daily reproductive turnover that is unusual among catostomids of comparable dimensions.

The incubation period for the demersal, adhesive eggs is brief, and upon hatching the yolk-sac larva emerges with a wet weight at birth of only 0.0031 grams [Wwb = 0.0031 grams]. This minute initial mass is consistent with the small egg diameter of 1.8 millimeters from which it derives. Rapid yolk absorption and the onset of exogenous feeding follow within a few days, after which the pelagic larva enters a phase of accelerated growth. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult reaches 1,150 grams [Wwi = 1,150 grams], a value that substantially exceeds the mass at puberty by a factor of roughly fifteen, indicating a prolonged period of somatic investment after sexual maturation has been initiated. Comparative data from other members of the family Catostomidae suggest that this magnitude of post-pubertal growth is not unusual for medium-bodied suckers inhabiting productive lowland streams.

Maximum recorded longevity for the Creek chubsucker stands at approximately 2,555 days [am = approximately 2,555 days] when assessed under the prevailing 18 °C [T = 18 °C] conditions of their native range. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly seven years, places the species within the typical range observed for other iteroparous catostomids of moderate body size. Age validation through otolith annuli confirms that individuals can persist through multiple reproductive seasons, with the oldest documented specimen exceeding this benchmark by a narrow margin. Senescence is gradual, and reproductively active adults retain spawning condition until the final year of life, after which post-reproductive mortality ensues from a combination of physiological deterioration and increased vulnerability to predation. The steady thermal regime of their habitat likely contributes to the consistent age structure observed across different populations.

Reproductive output, integrated over the entire lifespan, is considerable. Field estimates indicate that under the 18 °C [T = 18 °C] conditions typical of spawning grounds, a female can release approximately 79 eggs in a single event, and given the near-daily spawning frequency, the cumulative fecundity across one reproductive season can surpass many tens of thousands of oocytes. The daily reproductive rate calculated from these observations equates to roughly 79 eggs per day, a parameter that reflects the species' strategy of producing numerous small offspring rather than investing heavily in individual young. This high fecundity is balanced by elevated mortality during the early larval stages, when planktonic drift and predation pressure exert strong selective forces on the cohort. Survivorship curves constructed from mark-recapture data indicate a Type III pattern, with steep losses in the first weeks post-hatching.

Adult habitat use centers on slow-moving pools and backwater areas of Coastal Plain streams, where substrate composition and detrital food webs support the energetic demands of sustained growth and reproduction. Water temperatures in these systems rarely deviate from the 18 °C [T = 18 °C] optimum, which appears to synchronize gonadal recrudescence with seasonal peaks in invertebrate prey availability. Dietary analyses reveal a generalist feeding strategy, with benthic macroinvertebrates, particularly chironomid larvae and ephemeropteran nymphs, constituting the bulk of ingested matter. The species' relatively modest ultimate length of 41.9 centimeters [Li = 41.9 centimeters] may reflect a trade-off between maximizing fecundity and minimizing the metabolic costs of maintaining a large body in warm, sometimes hypoxic waters. Ongoing monitoring programs continue to refine estimates of age-specific growth and mortality, providing a robust framework for understanding the life history ecology of this resilient catostomid.
